As a result, the rela- tive proportions of the asset classes will vary over time as the capital markets move, producing an undesirable variation in the portfolio's risk and return characteristics. In the short run, it also will result in being wrong at every major market turn. For example, with a buy-andhold strategy, a portfolio's allocation to U.S. stocks reaches its maximum as a U.S. stock bull market ends and a bear market begins. Conversely, the allocation to U.S. stocks will be at its minimum at the end of a bear market, as the next bull market gets under way. In the long run, a buy-and-hold strategy also likely will result in an increasingly greater percentage of the portfolio being committed to equities because of their higher expected returns. This produces an undesirable trend of increasing volatility exposure coupled with a shortening investment time horizon. By contrast, strategic asset allocation requires periodic portfolio rebalancing in order to maintain the target allocation to each asset

texts.label: text
texts.orig: class. Portfolio cash flow activity can be used to facilitate this rebalancing. If a client is withdrawing money from her portfolio, it can be taken from the asset class that is most overweight relative to its target allocation. If a client is adding money to the portfolio, it can be first invested in whichever asset class that is most underweight relative to its target allocation. Absent cash flow activity, money is reallocated periodically from the most recent better-performing asset classes to the relative underperformers. For example, during a bull market for U.S. stocks, such as occurred during the 1990s, the portfolio's commitment to U.S. stocks will become larger than its target allocation. Returning to the target allocation thus necessitates selling U.S. stocks during the bull market. Conversely, to maintain the target allocation to U.S. stocks during the bear market accompanying the Global Financial Crisis of 2008, U.S. stocks must be bought. Strategic asset allocation is thus contrarian in execution and inherently "buy low, sell high."

texts.orig: capital gains taxes and/or significant transaction costs. Under the federal income tax laws in effect at the time of this writing, if an investor holds an appreciated stock at the time of his death, the inheritor of the stock receives a stepped-up tax basis. The capital gains taxes attributable to the appreciation that occurred during the deceased's lifetime are eliminated. Obviously, a client's age and health therefore need to be considered when evaluating the disposition of an appreciated security. If the client in the example above, Mr. Smith, were terminally ill, retaining this stock probably would be advisable. When an investor evaluates whether he should hold an appreciated stock until his death, the choice entails either paying or not paying capital gains taxes. If, however, a client expects to eventually sell the appreciated stock at some point prior to his death, the choice is not to either pay the capital gains taxes or not pay the capital gains taxes. Rather, the choice is to either pay the taxes sooner or pay the taxes later. The question concerns the time value of money, where the economic cost involved with selling an appreciated security is equal to the difference between the taxes due if sold now and the discounted present value of the taxes due at the future time of sale—a much smaller economic cost to justify a move toward a better-diversified portfolio.

texts.orig: For this reason, it may be advisable to carry the security on the client's balance sheet at a lower value that adjusts for the anticipated taxes due upon sale. This accomplishes two things: First, it generates client awareness that the security should not be retained merely because its sale will trigger the current payment of capital gains taxes. Second, it avoids the perception of a decrease in net worth as a result of the sale of an appreciated security that is not expected to be held until death. When the issue is framed this way, a client may be less resistant to paying capital gains taxes in order to broaden the diversification of the portfolio and thereby improve its volatility-adjusted returns. Another complicating factor exists when the appreciated security has a substantial income yield. Although the government has a claim on the unrealized appreciation, the client nevertheless gets the entire income stream from the security. Consider a stock with a $26-per-share tax basis, now selling for $100 per share. If the stock pays $4 per year in dividends, its current income yield is 4 percent. Assume that, upon sale, 15 percent of the realized gain will be lost to capital gains taxes. Aftertax sale proceeds of $88.90 are available for repositioning. Sometimes, clients respond by saying that they do not want to leave a huge portfolio to their survivors, and so periodic invasions of principal are acceptable to them. The problem is that even an intentional full liquidation of principal may not increase sufficiently the cash flow available for meeting living expenses. For example, the widow with $2.5 million invested in certificates of deposit at 4 percent has an interest income of $100,000 per year. If, instead of spending only the interest, she systematically liquidates the principal over her 30-year life expectancy, her annual cash flow will increase to $144,575. This higher cash flow is not enough to compensate for a 3 percent inflationary environment that will increase the cost of living by 2.4 times over her remaining life expectancy. Ideally, it would be advisable to choose a real (that is, inflationadjusted) annual withdrawal rate that will maintain the purchasing power of the investment portfolio. At first blush, we seem to be able to achieve this goal by setting the annual portfolio withdrawal rate equal to the difference between the portfolio compound annual return and the inflation rate. To work reliably, however, the portfolio must have a constant rate of return—that is, a standard deviation equal to zero. For example, Exhibit 15.4 illustrates that, with a constant portfolio return of 5 percent and an inflation rate of 3 percent, the portfolio can sustain in perpetuity a real withdrawal rate of 2 percent. Although these returns are admittedly awful, a 1-year period is much too short a time horizon over which to evaluate equity performance. In the short run, the highly volatile nature of annual equity returns overwhelms the incremental reward an investor expects to earn on average for bearing volatility risk. As a result, equity investing is appropriate only for longer time horizons during which good years can offset bad years and the equity return advantage has an opportunity to emerge. Just as an equity holding period should be longer term, an equity strategy likewise is most appropriately evaluated over longer time horizons. So I suggested to my client that we evaluate strategic asset allocation over the 10-year period ending with 2008. The last column in Exhibit 16.1 shows the compound annual returns for each asset class over this 10-year period. Over intermedi- ate periods, we expect (and hope) that the asset classes will have dissimilar patterns of returns. This dissimilarity in returns among the asset classes drives the long-term superior performance of a broadly diversified strategy. Of the four equity asset classes, U.S. stocks had the worst return—a compound annual loss of –1.38 percent with dividend income reinvested. (This 10-year return for U.S. stocks was the worst from 1926 to the time of publication of this book.) At the time it was only the third instance since 1926 that U.S. stocks had had a 10-year compound annual loss. Fortunately for the multiple-asset-class investor, other equity asset classes fared much better. Real estate securities and commodity-linked securities generated compound annual returns of 7.42 percent and 7.35 percent, respectively. An investment in either of these asset classes more than doubled in value over the 10-year holding period—even after sustaining huge losses in 2008. texts.orig: was 2008! Now we will examine the second issue. During 2008, the four equity asset classes simultaneously had devastating losses. Is this not a failure of multiple-asset-class equity diversification? In Chapter 8, we found that diversification payoffs are generated in a portfolio when one asset class's below-average return is partially offset by another asset class's above-average return. Therefore let's define a diversification failure as a year in which all four equity asset classes simultaneously have below-average returns or above-average returns—that is, no equity asset class is zigging while others are zagging. Exhibit 16.3 lists seven such failures—three are "positive failures," and four are "negative failures." The fact that all four equity asset classes had below-average returns in 2008 was unusual but not without precedent. Some might argue that it is not a failure of diversification when all equity asset classes deliver above-average performance; yet the "positive failures" meet our definition of failure since no asset class zigged while others zagged. These "positive failures" of diversification differ only in that no one complains about them. Exhibit 16.3

texts.orig: the aftermath. The rewards of multiple-asset-class investing rely on dissimilarities in patterns of returns across the portfolio's asset classes. In a risk-on, risk-off market environment, investors tend to simultaneously buy all risky asset classes when turning optimistic and sell all risky asset classes when becoming pessimistic. This behavior is particularly acute when fear about the future is running high. As the old Wall Street saying goes: "The only things that go up in a panic are the correlations." With higher correlations among equity asset classes, the benefits of multiple-asset-class equity diversification are less. At the same time, however, when money retreats from the equity asset classes, it must go somewhere to seek safety. In the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis, the retreat was a "flight to quality" to the perceived safety of U.S. Treasury securities. So while the correlations among equity asset classes rose during the Global Financial Crisis, the correlations between equity asset classes and very high quality bonds dropped, underscoring the value of diversification into interest-generating investments. At some point in the future, many of our current economic problems will find some sort of resolution, and we may once again find that equity asset classes will display more dissimilarity in their patterns of returns. texts.orig: The capital markets never before have been in the hands of the world's politicians as much as is the case today. We must worry not just about the usual economic risks and market risks; we also must be concerned about the possibility that politicians will choose a path that takes us over a cliff. Policy makers face thorny issues that demand tough decisions: the burgeoning U.S. government debt, financial institutions that are "too big to fail and too complex to regulate," unresolved eurozone problems, to name a few. The best course of action is not always clear. For example, in the United States we currently have both a weak economy and a burgeoning debt crisis. Do we need more fiscal stimulus, or is it time for austerity? Even if agreement exists on the wisest course of action, do politicians have the political courage to enact policies that may be painful in the short run but necessary for longer-term economic health? Hopefully the world's policy makers will act preemptively with sufficient wisdom to prevent the unnecessary economic damage triggered by inaction. Too often, however, policy makers take action only when a crisis emerges that forces them to respond. In addition to the economic risks and market risks facing investors, behavioral risks also introduce the possibility of self-inflicted wounds.

texts.orig: In Chapter 5, we discussed the rise of tactical asset allocation following the Global Financial Crisis. Understandably, no one ever wants to again suffer equity asset class losses like those experienced in 2008. Hence, the promise of market timing and other tactical asset allocation strategies is appealing. For the reasons we discussed in Chapter 5, however, we think these tactical strategies most likely will be a detriment to portfolio performance. Investors and advisors look back at 2007 and berate themselves for not seeing the inevitable crisis that was developing. No doubt, there were people who saw and understood different aspects of the developing crisis, but the exact manner in which the crisis unfolded and the extent of the accompanying market and economic damage were not foreseen.

texts.orig: that tracks the performance of thousands of mutual funds covering a wide variety of investment strategies in both fixed-income and equity markets worldwide. Amazingly few mutual funds posted positive returns in 2008. Out of 3,734 funds that invest primarily in U.S. stocks, all but one lost money. (The single fund with a positive return was the Forester Value Fund with a total return of 0.4 percent. The fund was tiny, with only $60 million in total assets as of December 31, 2008.) The 978 funds that invest primarily in non-U.S. stocks all lost money. Every one of the 144 real estate security funds (both U.S. and nonU.S.) had negative returns. Out of 128 natural resource funds, which include those that invest in commodity-linked securities, all lost money. It was a tough year for equity investors, with all but one of the 4,984 equity mutual funds losing money. Fixed-income funds performed better but were also badly battered. Out of 1,730 bond funds, both taxable and municipal, 68 percent lost money. The bond funds with positive returns were mostly government bond funds and shortterm bond funds. The scope and severity of the emerging crisis was clearly unforeseen by almost everyone. I frankly do not like the current investment environment. Not much looks good to me right now. Risks are high and the expected returns are low for both interest-generating investments and equity investments. Nevertheless, as an investor and as an advisor, I must deal with the investment environment as it is and not as I want it to be. Despite my misgivings, as an investor I think I will be best served following a strategic asset allocation approach that utilizes multiple asset classes. As an advisor, I think this same approach will maximize the likelihood that my clients will reach their financial goals. Even though we can manage, mitigate, and modify risk, we cannot fully eliminate it. In the end, every portfolio still carries residual risk. As the former chairman of the Federal Reserve, Paul Volcker, said at a Chartered Financial Analyst conference many years ago: "You cannot hedge the world."

Clients often believe that, as professional advisors, we should have some method to eliminate the uncertainties that they find so difficult to live with comfortably. As we focus on the uncertainties inherent in investment management, however, all we can hope to accomplish is to get a better picture of the uncertainties—we cannot eliminate them. Whether it is a new markettiming guru or an investment idea that seems to promise better results than a well-diversified portfolio, clients will always face temptations that encourage them to depart from a well-conceived, long-term strategy. At times, adhering to strategic asset allocation decisions may seem dangerous, such as urging our clients to allocate more money to common stocks during a bear market in order to restore the proper balance in their portfolios. At other times, the equity commitment may become too great as a result of a market rise. To persuade clients to rebalance their portfolios back to target asset allocations in the midst of a bull market may sound like a parent telling a child that he has to leave a party just when everybody really starts to have fun. Historically, the money manager's job has been to enhance return and minimize risk by exercising superior skill in security selection and/or market timing. Success has been measured in terms of whether or not the manager has beaten the market. Since the superior talent of the money manager was presumed to be the engine driving portfolio performance, little attention was paid to the asset allocation decisions. Today, the capital markets are increasingly efficient, and it is dangerous to presume that superior skill can be safely relied on as the primary determinant of a portfolio's performance. texts.orig: we would do well to follow the advice of R. Buckminster Fuller, creator of the geodesic dome, who said, "Don't fight forces, use them." If investment management is simple but not easy, what are the implications for the investment advisory profession? Because it is sim- ple, advisors have a tremendous opportunity to add value for clients by properly educating them. Knowledgeable clients more likely will choose and remain committed to those strategies that are most appropriate for realizing their financial goals. In addition to being educators, we also must be architects and general contractors, designing and implementing broadly diversified investment strategies that we create in collaboration with our clients. Because investment management is not easy, we have important work to do on an ongoing basis. As the capital markets move, our services will be needed to provide our clients with perspective regarding their investment experience. Particularly during extreme market conditions, clients may need the discipline and assurance of a steady hand that urges them to remain committed to their long-term strategies. We have witnessed many changes in the world capital markets over the past several decades, and more changes will undoubtedly occur in the future. In this evolving investment environment, clients do not need sporadic investment suggestions. They need and will value the comprehensive management of their portfolios by knowledgeable investment professionals who are committed to their clients' financial well-being and willing to always act in their clients' best interests.
